newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong dollar under pressure as stocks plunge.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong dollar under pressure as stocks plunge.

text.p: The Hong Kong dollar is coming under increased selling pressure just four and a half months before the territory returns to Chinese control.
Rising political tension is undermining both the Hong Kong stock market and the local currency, which is pegged at a rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar, market pundits said on Thursday.
"At the moment I do not see any signs of any speculative pressure here but that is a nagging thing in people's minds," regional strategist Peter Churchouse said.
"There are some nagging political concerns here over the Bill of Rights and to some extent also the provisional legislative council," he said.
China has announced a plan to roll back a string of laws, including parts of the Bill of Rights, after it resumes sovereignty over Hong Kong at midnight on June 30.
The plan has prompted a wave of international objection and general weakness in the stock market.
The Hong Kong dollar has followed suit. Reflecting capital outflows, the unit jumped to a two-year high of HK$7.7500 on February 5 from a more usual level of HK$7.7375 on January 22.
Rumours about the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping sparked heavy selling in both markets on Thursday.

The Hang Seng Index fell 1.65 percent to 13,239.95 points, compared to an all-time closing high of 13,868.24 on January 20, while the Hong Kong dollar suddenly soared back up to HK$7.7497 from HK$7.7461 at about 0800 GMT.
"The fluctuation in the Hong Kong dollar is related to the stock market sell-off," said Dong Tao, chief economist at Schroders Securities Asia.
"The market is getting exhausted and looking for a reason to sell. People were looking for an excuse and the Deng rumour served that purpose," Tao said.
Wilson Leung, technical analyst at Trendsetter Financial Services Ltd, is forecasting a rise in the Hong Kong dollar to at least HK$7.7550 and possibly HK$7.7760.
"Technically, the trend has turned bullish on the U.S. dollar," Leung said.
The unit is trading at its weakest level since an opportunistic attack following the Mexican peso crisis in January 1995, which took the currency to HK$7.7720.

The territory's de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), immediately raised interest rates to punishing levels during the 1995 assault, but dealers reported no intervention on Thursday.

The HKMA is well-defended against any speculative attack, with more than US$60 billion in foreign exchange reserves as well as a fistful of repurchase agreements with other Asian nations. Many are sitting of huge caches of foreign exchange.

This substantial war chest and repeated warnings to speculators by Joseph Yam, the HKMA's chief executive, are the source of much comfort to Hong Kong residents proud of their currency's stability through some turbulent times.
"As the lender of last resort for Hong Kong dollars, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will not lend cheaply, directly or indirectly, to speculators," Yam said late last year.

But Schroder's Tao warns the Hong Kong dollar is not completely safe. Typical of much of Asia, Hong Kong enjoys a high savings rate of 36 percent, most of it placed in short-term banking deposits that hold more than US$250 billion.

If local residents get scared, this vast, liquid treasure chest could be switched into foreign exchange with the touch of a button at automatic cash machines around the territory and quickly exhaust the territory's financial reserves.
"The danger is from within. Liquidity is extremely high. If there are problems, it could fly off very rapidly," he said.
Political commentators declined to speculate on the sort of event that could precipitate this sort of activity except to say it would have to be much worse than anything witnessed so far.
Although many market experts believe Deng's death has been discounted, others said it could herald a period of political uncertainty in China and market nervousness.
Some economists also warn of infectious currency weakness.

"There are a couple of (Asian) currencies having difficulty right now," said one economist. "If one of these currencies goes down, then people holding Hong Kong dollar assets might start to worry about it, compare themselves to that currency, and this could cause a shift in deposits."
Both the Thai baht and South Korean won have come under heavy speculative pressure in recent weeks.
